client: I've been feeling really overwhelmed lately, mostly because of this new job I started a few months ago. Last week during a team meeting, a colleague actually called out some mistakes I made in front of everyone, and I haven't been able to stop thinking about it since. I'm not sure talking about it is really going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It takes real courage to give this a shot even when you're not sure it will help, and I'm really glad you're here. Being called out in front of your team like that sounds genuinely humiliating and painful, and it makes complete sense that your mind keeps returning to that moment. I'm curious — when you replay that situation, what's the thought that tends to show up most strongly for you?

client: The thought that keeps coming back is basically "everyone in that room now thinks I'm incompetent." It's like I can't shake the feeling that I've already ruined my reputation at this job and it's only been a few months. And the worst part is, I'm not even sure the colleague was entirely wrong, which makes it feel even harder to just let it go.
therapist: That thought — "everyone thinks I'm incompetent" — sounds absolutely exhausting to carry around, and it makes sense it's hard to shake, especially when part of you feels like the criticism had some truth to it. It's worth gently noticing, though, that making mistakes a few months into a new job is actually very normal, and one difficult moment rarely defines how an entire room full of people sees you. When you imagine what your colleagues were actually thinking in that meeting, is there any evidence that supports a different interpretation than the one your mind jumped to?

client: I mean, maybe a couple of people looked a little uncomfortable when it happened, like they weren't totally okay with how it was handled. But I keep second-guessing that interpretation, like maybe I'm just telling myself that to feel better rather than seeing things clearly. It's hard to trust my own read on the situation when I'm this anxious about it.
therapist: The fact that you're questioning your own perceptions actually shows really careful, honest thinking — but anxiety has a way of making us distrust the evidence that *doesn't* confirm our fears, while accepting the worst-case interpretation without question. Those colleagues who looked uncomfortable are real data too, and they deserve just as much weight as the anxious voice telling you it was all in your head. What do you think it would take for you to feel like you could trust your own observations a little more?

client: Honestly, I'm not sure what it would take, because the anxiety feels like it's kind of baked into how I see everything right now. Like even if I tried to consciously remind myself that those uncomfortable looks were real, part of me would just dismiss it as wishful thinking. I guess I don't really have a good answer to that question, which is a little frustrating.
therapist: It's actually really meaningful that you can see that pattern so clearly — noticing that anxiety is coloring your whole lens right now is an important insight, not a failure to have the right answer. Rather than trying to think your way out of it in the moment, sometimes it helps to gather small, real-world evidence over time that can slowly build a more balanced picture. I'm wondering — in the weeks since the meeting, have there been any interactions with your colleagues, even small ones, that felt neutral or positive?

client: There have been a couple of small things, like one colleague asked for my input on something last week, and another one said good morning and actually stopped to chat for a minute. But when I notice those things, my brain immediately jumps to "well, they're just being polite" or "they don't actually think you're capable," so it's like the positive evidence gets neutralized before it even has a chance to land. I can see what you're pointing at with gathering evidence over time, but I'm skeptical it'll be enough to quiet that voice that keeps undermining everything.
therapist: You're doing something really sharp right now — you're catching your mind in the act of neutralizing positive evidence, which is actually a really important pattern to recognize called "discounting the positive." It's worth asking: if a friend described those same interactions to you — a colleague seeking their input, another stopping to genuinely chat — would you so quickly dismiss those as "just politeness," or would you see them as meaningful signals? I'm curious what it would feel like to hold those small moments as *at least* as valid as the anxious interpretations, even just as an experiment.

client: If a friend told me those same things, I'd probably say "see, people don't think you're incompetent, they're clearly still engaging with you." So I can see the double standard there, and it's a little uncomfortable to admit that I'm harder on myself than I would be on anyone else. But holding those moments as equally valid feels almost impossible in practice, like intellectually I get it but emotionally it just doesn't stick.
therapist: That gap between knowing something intellectually and feeling it emotionally is one of the most common and frustrating experiences people have, and it doesn't mean you're doing anything wrong — it just means the anxious patterns have had a lot more practice than the compassionate ones. The self-compassion you'd naturally offer a friend is actually already inside you, which is a really hopeful sign, even if it feels out of reach right now. What do you think gets in the way of extending even a small fraction of that same kindness to yourself?

client: I think part of what gets in the way is this feeling that if I'm too easy on myself, I'll stop trying to improve or I'll miss real problems that I actually need to fix. Like self-compassion almost feels dangerous, as if it's the same thing as making excuses for myself. And honestly, growing up I don't think I got a lot of modeling for that kind of self-kindness, so it just feels really foreign and uncomfortable.
therapist: That belief — that self-compassion and accountability are opposites — is really common, but the research and lived experience of many people actually suggests the reverse: that harsh self-criticism tends to increase anxiety and avoidance, while self-compassion creates a safer internal environment to honestly face and learn from mistakes. It also makes so much sense that this feels foreign given what you grew up with, because we really do learn how to treat ourselves largely from how we were treated. I'm curious — can you think of a time, even a small one, where being kind to yourself actually helped you move forward rather than letting you off the hook?

client: I'm sitting here trying to think of an example and honestly struggling to come up with one, which itself feels kind of telling. Maybe there have been times where I gave myself a break when I was sick or going through something hard, and I didn't completely fall apart or become lazy, but it's hard to connect that to something like a work situation where the stakes feel higher. I guess I'm just not convinced yet that what works in lower-stakes moments would actually translate to something like this job situation where I feel like I have so much more to lose.
therapist: The fact that you *did* find an example — giving yourself a break during hard times and not falling apart — is actually more significant than it might feel right now, because it's real evidence that self-compassion didn't make you collapse or stop caring. It makes sense that the job feels different because the stakes feel higher, but it's worth considering whether the stakes being higher might actually be a reason *for* more self-compassion, not less, since you're navigating something genuinely challenging and new. What do you think would happen — in your worst fear — if you tried approaching one small moment at work this week with the same grace you'd give yourself when you're sick?

client: I think my worst fear is that I'd let my guard down, make another visible mistake, and then have even more evidence that I don't belong there. It's like self-compassion feels okay when I'm sick because being sick isn't my fault, but at work the mistakes feel like they are my fault, so I feel like I deserve the harshness in a way. I'm willing to try noticing one small moment this week, but I'm honestly not sure I'll be able to stop the self-critical voice from taking over before the self-compassion even gets a chance.
therapist: That phrase — "I deserve the harshness" — is really worth sitting with, because it reveals something important: the self-criticism isn't just a strategy to improve, it feels like a punishment you believe you've earned, which is a much heavier thing to carry. And the fact that you're willing to try noticing one small moment this week, even with all this doubt, shows a kind of courage that deserves recognition. When that self-critical voice does show up this week, I wonder if instead of trying to silence it, you could just notice it with curiosity — like "there's that voice again" — without letting it have the final word?

client: That reframe of noticing the voice without letting it have the final word feels a little more manageable than trying to replace it with something positive, which always feels forced to me. But I'm a little worried that "there's that voice again" might just become another way of dismissing something I actually need to pay attention to, like what if the voice is pointing to a real problem I should be fixing. I guess I'm not totally sure how to tell the difference between useful self-reflection and the kind of harsh self-criticism you're describing.
therapist: That's such a genuinely important distinction to make, and it shows real thoughtfulness that you're not just accepting the reframe at face value. A useful rule of thumb from CBT is that healthy self-reflection tends to be specific, actionable, and moves you forward — like "I should double-check my work before the next meeting" — while harsh self-criticism tends to be global, repetitive, and keeps you stuck, like "I'm incompetent and don't belong here." When that voice shows up this week, I wonder if you could ask it one simple question: "Is this giving me something useful I can actually do, or is it just making me feel worse?"
